overview.title: Versatility and reusability; the age of generative AI and self-supervised foundation models
overview.section: 1.9 What deep learning has achieved so far
overview.main_topic: End of section 1.7 (scalability via batch training; versatility and reusability, foundation models); section 1.8 on generative AI: foundation models trained by self-supervised reconstruction, their scale, the 'fuzzy database' view and prompting, and the long history of generative AI; opening of section 1.9
overview.central_idea: Deep learning models can keep learning from new data and be repurposed for new tasks — the idea behind foundation models. Generative AI is powered by very large foundation models trained by self-supervised learning, where the targets are taken from the input itself (reconstruct a noisy image, predict the next word), which removes the labeling bottleneck and unlocks unprecedented scale; such models act as a fuzzy database of human knowledge that can be queried by prompting.
overview.importance: This page connects the chapter's foundational picture (inputs, targets, loss, Figure 1.8) to the most visible deep learning systems of the day. The one-sentence definition of self-supervised learning — targets taken from the input — is the conceptual key to chapters 16–18 (text generation, image generation) and to the notion of foundation models used throughout the second half of the book.
learning_objectives: Explain why batch-wise training lets deep learning models use datasets of arbitrary size and what the remaining bottleneck is.
State the two aspects of 'versatility and reusability' (continued training without restarting; repurposability) and define a foundation model.
Define self-supervised learning in terms of Figure 1.8 and give the two reconstruction examples the page mentions.
Explain why removing manual annotation unlocked scale, and quote the page's orders of magnitude (parameters, data, cost).
Describe the 'fuzzy database' view of foundation models and what prompting means in that view.
Place generative AI in historical context: 1990s experiments, the 2017 first edition's chapter, mainstream awareness in 2022.
prerequisites: The training loop and Figure 1.8–1.9: predictions, true targets, loss (p.33–34)
Simplicity and scalability as properties of deep learning (p.34)

summary:
**Scalability, concluded.** Deep learning models are trained by iterating over small batches of data, so they can be trained on datasets of arbitrary size; the only bottleneck is the amount of parallel computational power, which, thanks to Moore's law, is 'a fast-moving barrier'.

**Versatility and reusability.** Unlike many prior approaches, deep learning models can be trained on *additional* data without restarting from scratch, which makes continuous online learning viable — important for very large production models. Trained models are also *repurposable* and thus reusable: this is the big idea behind **foundation models**, large models trained on humongous amounts of data that can be used across many new tasks with little or no retraining.

**1.8 The age of generative AI.** The best-known deep learning systems today are generative AI applications — chatbot assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) and image generators (Midjourney) — which produce informative or creative content from simple prompts, blurring the line between human and machine creativity. They are powered by very large foundation models that learn to *reconstruct* the text and image content fed to them: reconstruct a sharp image from a noisy version, predict the next word in a sentence. In terms of Figure 1.8, the **targets are taken from the input itself**: this is **self-supervised learning**, and it lets models use vast amounts of *unlabeled* data. Dropping the manual annotation that bottlenecked earlier machine learning unlocked unprecedented scale: some foundation models have hundreds of billions of parameters, are trained on over 1 petabyte of data, and cost tens of millions of dollars. These models act as a kind of **fuzzy database of human knowledge**, usable for a very wide range of applications without special-purpose programming or retraining: having memorized so much, they solve new problems via **prompting** — querying their learned knowledge representations and returning the output most likely to be associated with the prompt. Generative AI reached mainstream awareness in 2022 but has a long history: text generation experiments date to the 1990s, and the first edition of this book (2017) already had a hefty 'Generative AI' chapter predicting that much cultural content would 'soon' be created with AI's help.

**1.9 What deep learning has achieved so far** opens: over the past decade deep learning has produced a technological revolution, starting with remarkable results on perceptual tasks from 2013 to 2017 (continued on p.36).

paragraphs.what_it_says: Completing the Scalability bullet: deep learning models are trained by iterating over small batches of data, so they can be trained on datasets of arbitrary size. The only bottleneck is parallel computational power, which Moore's law keeps pushing back.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Because each training step touches only a small batch, the whole dataset never has to fit in memory or be processed at once; more data simply means more batches. Dataset size therefore stops being a limit on what can be learned; compute is the limit, and compute keeps growing.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the second half of the scalability argument and the mechanical reason foundation models (next bullet) can be trained on over a petabyte of data (later on this page).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book on this page): batch-wise training is mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (p.68): each weight update uses the loss on a small random batch, so an epoch over a huge dataset is just many such updates.

terminology.meaning: A small subset of the training data processed in one iteration of the training loop.

connections: p.34: the start of the Scalability bullet — parallelization on GPUs and specialized hardware.
p.68: mini-batch stochastic gradient descent, the procedure that 'iterates over small batches of data'.

paragraphs.excerpt: Versatility and reusability—Unlike many prior machine learning approaches, deep learning
paragraphs.what_it_says: Deep learning models can be trained on additional data without restarting from scratch, which makes continuous online learning viable — important for very large production models. Trained models are also repurposable and hence reusable, which is the big idea behind foundation models: large models trained on humongous amounts of data, usable across many new tasks with little or no retraining.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Two consequences of 'knowledge lives in the weights'. First, because training is incremental (the loop of Figure 1.9 can simply be continued), new data can be absorbed without discarding what was learned. Second, the representations a model has learned for one task are often useful for others, so a trained model is an asset to be reused rather than a one-off. Foundation models push this to the extreme: train once at enormous scale, reuse everywhere.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Reusability is the premise of transfer learning (chapter 8, p.266: pretrained vision models 'can be used to bootstrap powerful vision models out of very little data') and of the whole LLM-centred second half of the book (p.525 defines foundation models formally).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book on this page): 'without restarting from scratch' works because the optimizer only needs the current weights and new batches; there is no fixed training set the model depends on. Repurposing typically means keeping the learned layers and continuing training (fine-tuning) on a new task, or using the model as is (p.525).

paragraphs.excerpt: Generative AI is powered by very large “foundation models” that learn to reconstruct
paragraphs.what_it_says: Three printed paragraphs. (1) Generative AI runs on very large foundation models that learn to *reconstruct* the content fed to them — a sharp image from a noisy version, the next word of a sentence. In Figure 1.8's terms, the targets are taken from the input itself: *self-supervised learning*, which lets models use vast amounts of unlabeled data. Removing the annotation bottleneck unlocked unprecedented scale: hundreds of billions of parameters, over 1 petabyte of training data, tens of millions of dollars. (2) These models act as a fuzzy database of human knowledge, applicable widely without special-purpose programming or retraining; having memorized so much, they solve new problems via *prompting* — querying their learned knowledge representations and returning the output most likely associated with the prompt. (3) Generative AI became mainstream in 2022 but is old: text generation experiments date to the 1990s, and the 2017 first edition had a hefty 'Generative AI' chapter predicting that 'soon' much cultural content would be AI-assisted.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The crucial move is the reinterpretation of Figure 1.8. Supervised learning needs a human to supply the true target Y for each input X. In self-supervised learning the data supplies its own targets: hide or corrupt part of an input, and the hidden part *is* the target. Every sentence on the internet becomes a training example for next-word prediction with no annotator in the loop — hence 'vast amounts of unlabeled data' and the scale figures. The 'fuzzy database' metaphor then explains the user-facing behavior: a model that has reconstructed so much text has, in effect, stored a compressed, approximate copy of it, and a prompt is a query that retrieves the most likely continuation. The history paragraph tempers the novelty: the mechanism is decades old; what changed is scale.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the first appearance of self-supervised learning and foundation models, the two ideas on which chapters 16–18 (text generation, image generation, LLMs) rest. It also answers a question many readers bring to the book — why do chatbots seem to know everything? — with a mechanistic, non-mystical explanation consistent with p.31's insistence that deep learning is just mathematics plus data.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book on this page): next-word prediction is still a loss between predictions Y' and targets Y exactly as in Figure 1.8 — the model outputs a probability for each possible next token and the target is the token that actually followed; denoising is likewise a reconstruction loss between the model's output and the clean image. p.525 calls this 'a self-supervised learning objective (a reconstruction loss)'. 'Fuzzy' is a deliberate hedge: retrieval is approximate and probabilistic, not exact lookup.

concepts.name: Foundation model
concepts.definition: A large model trained on humongous amounts of data that can be used across many new tasks with little retraining, or even none at all.
concepts.intuition: Train once at enormous scale, reuse everywhere.
concepts.technical: Trained by self-supervised reconstruction of text or image content; some have hundreds of billions of parameters, over 1 petabyte of training data, and cost tens of millions of dollars. Formally (p.525): trained on broad data, generally with self-supervision at scale, fine-tunable to a wide range of downstream tasks.
concepts.significance: The 'big idea' behind deep learning's reusability and the engine of generative AI.
concepts.example: The models behind ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Midjourney.
concepts.misconception: A foundation model is not programmed for each application; it is reused via prompting or light fine-tuning.

concepts.name: Self-supervised learning
concepts.definition: Learning in which the targets of Figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself — the model learns to reconstruct its input (a sharp image from a noisy one, the next word in a sentence).
concepts.intuition: The data labels itself: hide part of it and ask the model to fill it in.
concepts.technical: A reconstruction loss between the model's output and the withheld or clean part of the input; no human annotation is needed, so vast amounts of unlabeled data can be used.
concepts.significance: It removed the annotation bottleneck of earlier machine learning and unlocked the scale of foundation models.
concepts.example: Next-word prediction on text; denoising on images.
concepts.misconception: Self-supervised learning is not 'learning without a loss' or without targets; it uses exactly the loss setup of Figure 1.8, with targets derived from the data rather than from annotators.

concepts.name: Prompting
concepts.definition: Solving a new problem by querying the knowledge representations a foundation model has learned and returning the output most likely to be associated with the prompt.
concepts.intuition: Asking a fuzzy database a question in natural language.
concepts.technical: Because the model has memorized so much during reconstruction training, a prompt elicits the most probable continuation or completion, with no special-purpose programming or retraining.
concepts.significance: It is why one foundation model serves a very wide range of applications.
concepts.example: Typing a question into a chatbot assistant and receiving an informative answer.
concepts.misconception: The model is not looking up an exact record; the 'database' is fuzzy, so outputs are probabilistic approximations of what it has seen.

concepts.name: Generative AI
concepts.definition: Deep learning applications — chatbot assistants, image generation services — that produce informative or creative content in response to simple prompts.
concepts.intuition: Models that output new content rather than a label.
concepts.technical: Powered by very large foundation models trained by self-supervised reconstruction (p.620: capable of generating text, images, videos or sound).
concepts.significance: The most visible success of deep learning and the subject of chapters 16–18.
concepts.misconception: Generative AI is not new to 2022: text generation experiments date to the 1990s and the 2017 edition of this book already covered it.

concepts.name: Versatility and reusability
concepts.definition: Deep learning models can be trained on additional data without restarting from scratch (continuous online learning) and are repurposable for new tasks.
concepts.intuition: What a model learned is kept in its weights and can be extended or redirected.
concepts.technical: Training is incremental, so new batches can be added at any time; learned representations transfer to other tasks (p.266).
concepts.significance: The third property that makes deep learning different (section 1.7) and the basis of foundation models.
concepts.example: A pretrained image classifier reused to build a vision model from very little data (p.266).
concepts.misconception: Reusability does not mean a model works on any task unchanged; often a little retraining is needed, sometimes none.

deeper.title: Figure 1.8 with the target taken from the input
deeper.body: Take the sentence 'the cat sat on the mat'. For next-word prediction: (1) Input X = 'the cat sat on the'; (2) True target Y = 'mat' — not written by an annotator, just the word that actually came next; (3) the model produces Predictions Y' (a score for every possible next word); (4) the Loss function compares Y' with Y and the optimizer adjusts the weights, exactly as in Figures 1.8–1.9. Every position in every sentence of a text corpus gives one such example for free. For image denoising: X = the image with noise added, Y = the original image, Y' = the model's reconstruction. In both cases 'the targets from figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself'. (Worked example not in the book; the mechanism is as the page describes.)

deeper.title: Why dropping annotation changes the scale by orders of magnitude
deeper.body: Beyond the book: supervised datasets are bounded by labeling effort — every example costs human time, so even large labeled datasets have on the order of millions of examples. Self-supervised data is bounded only by how much raw text or imagery exists; the page's 'over 1 petabyte' is possible because nobody had to annotate any of it. More data justifies more parameters (hundreds of billions), and more parameters and data cost more compute (tens of millions of dollars). The page's three numbers are three faces of the same removal of the annotation bottleneck.

deeper.title: The 'fuzzy database' metaphor, and its limits
deeper.body: A conventional database returns exact records for exact queries and nothing for anything it has not stored. A foundation model is 'fuzzy' in both directions: it answers paraphrased or novel queries by returning what is *most likely associated* with them, and its 'records' are statistical regularities rather than stored strings. That is why one model can serve many applications without retraining — and also why its answers are approximate rather than guaranteed. The metaphor is the authors'; the observation about approximation is an interpretation consistent with their word 'fuzzy'.

misconceptions.claim: Self-supervised models learn without any targets or loss function.
misconceptions.correction: They use the same loss setup as Figure 1.8; the difference is that the targets are taken from the input itself (the next word, the clean image) rather than supplied by annotators.

misconceptions.claim: Generative AI appeared out of nowhere in 2022.
misconceptions.correction: The page says it only rose to mainstream awareness in 2022; text generation experiments go back to the 1990s and the 2017 first edition of this book already had a hefty generative AI chapter.

misconceptions.claim: A foundation model must be reprogrammed or retrained for each new application.
misconceptions.correction: The page says these models are amenable to a very wide range of applications without special-purpose programming or retraining; they are used via prompting.

misconceptions.claim: Dataset size is a hard limit on what deep learning can learn.
misconceptions.correction: Because training iterates over small batches, datasets of arbitrary size can be used; the only bottleneck is parallel compute.

takeaways: Batch-wise training means datasets of any size can be used; the only bottleneck is parallel compute.
Deep learning models can keep learning from new data without restarting and can be repurposed — the big idea behind foundation models.

Generative AI is powered by very large foundation models trained by self-supervised learning: the targets of Figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself (next word, clean image), so unlabeled data at petabyte scale can be used.
Foundation models act as a fuzzy database of human knowledge, queried by prompting, with no special-purpose programming or retraining.
Generative AI went mainstream in 2022 but its roots go back to the 1990s and it was already in this book's 2017 first edition; the deep learning revolution began with perceptual tasks in 2013–2017.

questions.question: How does the page define self-supervised learning?
options: Learning in which the targets of Figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself
Learning in which a model labels data for another model
Learning that requires manually annotated targets for every example
questions.answer: Learning in which the targets of Figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself
questions.explanation: The page says foundation models learn to reconstruct the content fed to them, which 'means that the targets from figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself. This is referred to as self-supervised learning.' A loss is still used; no second model or annotators are involved.

questions.question: Give the two reconstruction tasks the page uses as examples of what foundation models learn.
questions.answer: Reconstructing a sharp image from a noisy version, and predicting the next word in a sentence.
questions.explanation: Both are listed in the sentence describing how foundation models 'learn to reconstruct the text and image content fed into them'.

questions.question: Explain the causal chain the page draws from self-supervised learning to the scale of modern foundation models.
questions.answer: Because targets come from the input itself, no manual annotation is needed, so models can use vast amounts of unlabeled data; removing the annotation bottleneck of earlier machine learning unlocked unprecedented scale — hundreds of billions of parameters, over 1 petabyte of training data, costs of tens of millions of dollars.
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says doing away with manual annotations 'has unlocked a level of scale never seen before' and gives those three figures.

questions.question: What does the page mean by saying foundation models can solve new problems 'merely via prompting'?
options: The model is retrained on the prompt before answering
The prompt is compiled into special-purpose code
The prompt queries the knowledge representations the model has learned, and the model returns the output most likely associated with it
The model looks up the prompt in an exact database of stored answers
questions.answer: The prompt queries the knowledge representations the model has learned, and the model returns the output most likely associated with it
questions.explanation: This is the page's description of prompting. It stresses that no retraining or special-purpose programming is needed, and the database metaphor is explicitly 'fuzzy', not exact lookup.

questions.question: What two things does 'versatility and reusability' refer to, and what single idea does the page say grows out of reusability?
questions.answer: Models can be trained on additional data without restarting from scratch (continuous online learning), and trained models are repurposable; reusability is the big idea behind foundation models.
questions.explanation: Both halves and the link to foundation models are in the bullet.

questions.question: The page says the only bottleneck for training on huge datasets is parallel compute. Why is dataset size itself not a bottleneck?
questions.answer: Because deep learning models are trained by iterating over small batches of data, so the data never has to be processed all at once; a larger dataset just means more batches, which is a compute cost, not a structural limit.
questions.explanation: The page states that batch-wise training allows 'datasets of arbitrary size' and that the only bottleneck is parallel computational power.

questions.question: Can you place generative AI on the timeline the page gives (1990s, 2017, 2022, 2013–2017) and say what happened at each point?
questions.answer: 1990s: earliest text generation experiments; 2013–2017: remarkable deep learning results on perceptual tasks; 2017: the first edition of this book already had a generative AI chapter; 2022: generative AI rose to mainstream awareness.
questions.explanation: A self-check on the historical framing of sections 1.8 and 1.9.

questions.question: Which generative AI products does the page name?
questions.answer: Chatbot assistants ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, and the image generation service Midjourney.
